description: The first cluster identified in this network presents two papers, Shanteau et al. (2002) and Ye and Johnson (1995), which concentrate a greater number of citations, compared to the other papers within this cluster. However, these works are not the most connected. In this sense, Davis (1996) shows a more important role as a broker in the construction of the cluster. Another characteristic of this cluster is that most papers were published before the year 2000 (only two after that date). After reading the papers in the cluster, the expert systems configured the core of the topics covered by these, mainly related to experience and knowledge transfer.

The second cluster is located to the left of the former. In this cluster, the work by Dimitras et al. (1996) presents 292 citations, configuring the core of the group around the need to predict failure of companies. This work is a revision of the different predictive methods, with an emphasis on expert systems. In a similar vein, Olson and Mossman (2003) used neural networks with a similar objective. In general, the papers within this cluster pursue the prevision and advance in the prediction of bankruptcy (McKee & Greenstein, 2000), with different techniques that conform the initial steps in AI and BD analysis in the fields of auditing and accounting.

Cluster 3 is at the other extreme of the figure. In this cluster, there is an eclectic group of papers with a dispersed structure. A subgroup within this cluster presents a clear orientation towards the application of new technologies in the field of learning, with papers related to the education and teaching programmes of auditing and accounting. All these studies are related to Boyce et al. (2012), which, in turn, becomes a bridge to the rest of the cluster. In this part of the cluster, Jeacle and Carter (2011), Jones and Dugdale (2002), and Bebbington and Unerman (2018) are the authors who receive the highest number of citations, and the work of Jan Bebbington is configured as having the most shared references. In this sense, her works opened the field towards the application of technologies to relationships and have been applied to different situations and counterparts

In the next cluster, the size of the nodes is reduced and presents a high density with many links among the components. The papers are very recent, with the oldest going back to 2017. Links of the works of Bebbington and Unerman (2018) and Arnaboldi et al. (2017), with the work by Moll and Yigitbasioglu (2019), represent a connection between Clusters 3 and 4. The explanation of this linkage can be found in the technology used in the paper, which is the use of BD and its application to accounting. In Cluster 4, we can infer how BD and AI are connected to the transformation of accounting and auditing professions (Al-Htaybat et al., 2018).

In Cluster 5, Vasarhelyi et al. (2015), D. Appelbaum et al. (2017a), and Cao et al. (2015), are the papers with the higher number of citations and they structure the literature within this group. The works by Appelbaum (D. A. Appelbaum et al., 2018; D. Appelbaum et al., 2017a) associate BD analysis with auditing activity, while Vasarhelyi et al. (2015) and Cao et al. (2015) focus on the application towards accounting.

Cluster 6 also contains works by SPANISH JOURNAL OF FINANCE AND ACCOUNTING / REVISTA ESPAÑOLA DE FINANCIACIÓN Y CONTABILIDAD 425 Appelbaum (Appelbaum, 2016; Appelbaum & Nehmer, 2020). This cluster covers business analytics with the application of BD, from both auditing and accounting perspectives. Thus, BD exposes the limitations of current technologies in the development of these tasks.

Cluster 7 presents a highly cited paper (Li, 2010). In this cluster, forwardlooking statements are introduced, and machine learning links to BD to improve the quality of the information used and how this information improves the different activities developed by auditors, for example, to predict fraud (Perols et al., 2017), and accountants, for example, to evaluate disclosures (Henry & Leone, 2016) or in the elaboration of standards (Krahel & Titera, 2015).
